blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
[Dr B] (affirmed)
My Lord, may the witness be seated?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, certainly, do sit down. But keep your voice up. Because apart from having screens behind you, the people over there and the people behind you have got to hear you, and as you know, sound waves won't travel through that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: My name is [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. And your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I am a consultant paediatrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you in a moment about events in June in 2015, when I think you were also a
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: paediatrician at the Countess of Chester. Can you recall, please, when you first qualified as a doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: In 1989.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And when did you become a consultant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. And when did you start at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: In 2005.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In 2005, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, specifically, please, I would like to ask you about events on the evening of 9 June 2015 into the early hours of 10 June.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Were you on duty that particular night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, I was on call.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were on call, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And specifically, please, about a baby called [Baby B], who I understand you had cause to see that night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us, please, what you can remember of that night back in 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: I cannot recall the events of that night. That was 7 years ago and my -- the questions that I will be answering are based on my having read the statement and the patient's notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So I don't have recollection of events from that night.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Have you had the opportunity to refresh your opportunity from those notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, we have an electronic document which may assist.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So if I can ask, please, first of all ask Mr Murphy to put up tile number 228, please, on [Baby B]'s sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: How would you have been summoned to the hospital by way of -- on call?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So basically on the -- in the ward there is a senior house officer and a registrar on call, and when they have cause for concern, they ask for the switchboard to contact me at home --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: -- or the consultant paediatrician at home, and we then -depending on -- sometimes it's just a phone call, they just want advice. Other times the switchboard calls us up and tells us to attend immediately, in which case we just drive in.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you remember which of those options it was that night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So from what I can see in the notes, I can -- it says that I was asked to attend.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So it might have been the switchboard telling me to come to the neonatal unit, it might have been the -- one of the neonatal nurses who would have called and just said, just make your way to the neonatal unit. Because I think it is unlikely it would have been the registrar themselves, given what was going on; they probably would have been busy with the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Now, we have got a tile on the screen entitled "fast bleep"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that seems to have gone out, if I can put it that way, at 00.37. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So the fast bleep basically -- so at home we are on call over the phone.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: It's either the landline or the mobile. So it would have been one of those.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: There is a bleep, but because different consultants live at different distances, the bleep doesn't work -- it probably would have worked where I lived at the time, but the contact, from what I recall with other contacts, would have been either through the mobile or the landline.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very good, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in that case would you have -- you would have travelled into the hospital presumably?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And given what you told us, perhaps we can go to your notes now, please, which are found in 4 at 233.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: First of all, do you recognise that document?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we can see the date in the left-hand column and what appears to be a time around about 2.40, is that, am?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes, 2.40 am, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So and then an explanation almost straightaway:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Written retrospectively from 12.50."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Called at home at 12.36 am.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Arrived at..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you take us through that now, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Okay. So do you want me to talk --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, if you can read and it explain if you can, if you can expand on what it says.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Basically, yes, I would have been called at 12.36 am and most probably I would have taken that time from my mobile call, the time it was logged, and then arrival time is approximate.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it takes me -- it used to take me about -- depending on the time of the evening/night/day, a 10 to 12-minute drive into hospital from where I lived.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that time I have said:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Baby tubed already by reg."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So there are a few abbreviations there. I do apologise. So tubed means the baby would have been intubated by the registrar, and then I have given a little bit of background that the baby suddenly went appear apnoeic. So apnoea means they stopped breathing.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pausing there, doctor: you arrive, you have seen that the baby has been intubated. We've heard about intubation and the note is "went apnoeic". Is that something that has been relayed to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is you assimilating what you're faced with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Carry on, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So I obviously arrived at 12.50, would have taken a brief background from the doctors and the nurses there, and assessed the baby and went -- didn't go back to writing the notes until I was happy that the baby was stable.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the baby had been apnoeic and had gone apnoeic suddenly, so they'd suddenly stopped breathing, and I have said that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Purple blotching of body all over with slowing of heart rate."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this would have been the registrar's account.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The baby was bagged. So this is --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, just take that a little slowly:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Purple blotching of body all over."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: This will have been the registrar's account?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So the baby had:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Purple blotching of the body all over with slowing of heart rate."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that would have been the background history I would have been given. When the registrar attended they bagged. So this is the Neopuff that's applied to the face with oxygen connected and then they're given some help with the breathing, and then they had been intubated by the registrar.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, and then a comment about the heart rate?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The heart rate improved. So the first indication that we get when heart rate is slow and the breathing is slow or not there, the first indication we get that things are getting back on track is that the heart rate starts to pick up, which then means that oxygen is now being pumped into the rest of the body and hopefully the breathing recovery will follow.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's a positive sign of improvement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: "Adrenaline not required."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I have made that note because when the heart rate drops below 60 and we give help with the bag and masking, trying to get the heart to restart, it's the first thing we do.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If that does not work, then the next step is giving adrenaline to bump start the heart, basically. So I have made a note that only bag and mask with oxygen did the job and the heart rate improved. Adrenaline was not needed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Then a reference to 10ml?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "10ml per 10kg bolus given."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the baby's perfusion wouldn't have been good and we check that by checking their capillary refill time, which essentially involves checking their circulation and their perfusion. If that is not good, then we give some fluid, which is normally 0.9% sodium chloride.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's normal saline and in babies we give 10ml aliquots of those. A 10ml/kg bolus of that had already been given by the registrar when I arrived.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So that had already been done? So again this is part of the history that has been related to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Now, your next line begins "Upon my arrival".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So is that as distinct from what you'd been told?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So by the time I arrived and assessed the baby -- so as I have made the note that the registrar had noted purple blotching of the body all over with slowing of the heart rate, that note I have made. What I document there is that I have seen that there is purple blotchiness to the right mid-abdomen and right hand, and the baby is pink and active.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So whilst it's been related to you above that it was all over when you got there, you've indicated right hand -you held up your right hand and the right abdomen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you have any independent recollection of that now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. If we carry on, if we can just scroll down, please, with -- I think it says --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So then I have given readings of how much oxygen the baby was in. So this is 40% oxygen saturations. This is what the baby's oxygen levels were. They were 100%.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oxygen levels in the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So basically there is the -- the ventilator is connected to the oxygen, which is going to the baby. So that was 40%. Then there is a saturation monitor attached to the baby which reads what the baby's oxygen levels are.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just pausing there, 40%, that's above what would normally be in air?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So normally we don't need any oxygen to breathe, and as far as I can recall, the baby had been in air, they hadn't been requiring any oxygen or any support with their breathing previous to becoming suddenly poorly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: And then they -- when I saw them, they might have been in more oxygen before, but we go on the saturation monitors. So 100% is the highest that anybody's saturation level can go, and we like to keep them about 95. So at 100%, I probably would have weaned them -- tweaked the oxygen down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So with that 40% oxygen, the baby was saturating 100%, so that's basically really good.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And their heart rate was 143, which is slightly above normal, but good, given that their heart -- their heart rate had been slow, and then it had picked up. So it was reassuring that the heart rate was 143.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. And then it looks like we have --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: A blood gas, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have got a different time in the left-hand column.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is this -- so we can see what -- is that what you first saw when you arrived and this is a subsequent note? Is that the way to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So what I have done is I have made a note of -- so if we go up, I came at 50 -- so I came at 12.50. So the gas would have been being done and that gas at just past 00.51 in the morning, that blood gas would have been taken with a capillary heel prick, and it gives numbers.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you want me to go through them?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, in the context of what they mean.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: In the context of what they mean. So basically when we do a blood gas, it tells us information about -- pH is what the -there is a normal range of pH in babies which -- is anything from 7.25 onwards is considered as acceptable.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pausing there, pH is acid and alkali balance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. So a 7.20 means that this was suboptimal, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where should it be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where should it be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Anything from 7.25 upwards is reasonable.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. PC02. This is the carbon dioxide level in the body. Again, there are normal ranges for that and for babies we say it's between 4 to 6.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So this a little bit high. The oxygen levels are 10.46.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is acceptable. They tend to be between 10 to 12 and upwards. Base excess is the acidity in the blood, which is minus 8.4.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then we check her glucose which is 7.5, which is normal. Lactate is an acid that's produced in response to low oxygen levels on exposure to what we call hypoxia, which can be due to a number of reasons.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And hypoxia is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Low oxygen levels that the body is exposed to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: -- for a period of time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at that point I have noted the gas. The 20.6 is the ventilator settings, so the machine that the baby was connected to. So when they're intubated, they are connected to a ventilator, and there are pressures that are used to inflate the lungs.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Now, we have heard a little bit about that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There are two numbers. The higher number is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The breathing in pressure.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the lower number is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The breathing out pressure. Called PIP and PEEP.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: And they are in 40% oxygen at the time. We had some blood tests back, which is a blood count. The blood count -- the white cell count is 8.4 which is okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Neutrophils are another type of cell that fight infection. They are 3.3. Lymphocytes are 4.5, again within normal limits. Platelets are, I have said, 103, and I have noted a small clump. I think this would have been reported when the lab either ran through the result or they put the result on there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So if there is a little clot or a clump, then the result of the platelet count is not accurate. It tends to be lower than what it actually is.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So we sort of look at that with -- we would probably repeat that blood test to reassure ourselves that this was a clump, but I wouldn't go and act on that result by doing an intervention without confirming that the platelets are actually low.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: However, a level of 103 is not so alarmingly low that I want to do something about immediately.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: CRP, so this is C-reactive protein. This as marker for infection, and less than 4 is normal. So it's 1, which means it's normal.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then the other results that are written there are coagulation or clotting profile.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: That is a prothrombin time. This is normal. APTT is normal. Fibrinogen is normal. So this gives us an idea if there is a problem or a bleeding tendency in the baby's bloodstream which can be due to a variety of reasons.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But those readings in that regard are normal?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Normal, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then the bottom lines, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So the bottom line:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Platelet and FFP had been requested but have held off in view of above results."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I may, can I give a little bit of background to why they would have been requested?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, please, slowly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So basically the evening before, I had reviewed this baby, I had reviewed [Baby B], and we had a background history of maternal antiphospholipid syndrome, and I had also been made aware that [Baby A], [Baby B]'s brother, had passed away.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As part of that there was obviously increased alertness and anxiety about what could be done in anticipation for [Baby B] to give us some help, and as part of that various consultants -- I think I have made a note in my previous notes that the haematologist from Alder Hey had been consulted, that how do we investigate [Baby B] further in light of mum's diagnosis, and obviously we would have made them aware of -- that [Baby A] had sadly passed away.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the obstetrician, so this is mother's obstetrician, had also been in contact with the specialists who had been treating the mother about -- I think one was in UCL and another one was in Great Ormond Street. So they had been consulted as well, and we had slightly different opinions from both of them.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Both the consultants at UCL and GOS who had treated the mother gave the opinion that they did not feel that maternal antiphospholipid syndrome would affect the babies in any way. So they didn't think that any further investigations were needed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The haematologist at Alder Hey suggested doing a full blood count and a test called D-dimers and a clotting profile.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: So this was the evening before. So when we are on call, we would go -- you know, if I start my on call at 4.30, I will go to the children's ward, I'll see the children there who need seeing, and I'll come to the neonatal unit and I'll touch base with what was going on. And the evening before I was consulted — well, these are the two opinions that we had been given.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would this have been at the start of the evening shift on the 9th? When you say the day before --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: The night before, so basically this is going into the 9th when I'm called at 00.36. The evening before I was on call and I would have come to the unit and these conversations had been carrying on during the day where the doctors were ringing the Alder Hey haematologist and the obstetrician had come back with the information about the UCL and the GOS haematologists.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I was presented with this information that the Alder Hey haematologist is saying do these tests. The two haematologists who had been involved in managing mother's condition have said that this condition shouldn't really have any repercussions for the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I also knew that in the daytime some contact had been made to find out about initial post-mortem findings for [Baby A], whether there was anything there that would help us help [Baby B], and I don't think there was anything available yet.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I had this information the night before and on balance, because [Baby B] was well, I decided to go with the UCL and GOS haematologists' advice and said, well, this is late evening now, [Baby B] is fine, let's leave these for now and we can come back and revisit this in the morning if need be.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That night, obviously, [Baby B] became poorly and they would have done a clotting and a blood count and they also did Ddimers. I think it comes later on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's the background to those tests being done at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They hadn't been done earlier because of the advice you'd had?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Done later at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. And because of that concern about maternal phospholipid syndrome, platelets and a fresh frozen plasma would have been requested, that if there is something going on, when we get the results back, rather than wasting the time, because it takes time to get those blood products, they're not like O negative blood that you can get literally immediately. So you have to request them and then there is a time lag before they arrive, and then they're given to the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay. But the results meant that you were holding off on those?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes. Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So -- sorry. There was something else you wanted to say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "So I have said" -- carry on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: So:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Platelets and FFP had been requested but have held off in view of above results and clinical improvement."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So in other words you just didn't know whether perhaps mother's condition might be affecting the children --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- and [Baby A], having died the night before, [Baby B] having taken ill, you were just, out of precaution doing this, but the results that you had were essentially good, there didn't appear to be any difficulty there, so that's why you did what you did?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you scroll up, please, for the rest of the note.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR B: Okay. So then I have written there:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Restarted on antibiotics."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So [Baby B] would have been screened initially and normally if there's no evidence of infection and the blood cultures are negative and the C-reactive protein results are normal as well, we would stop antibiotics after 36 to 48 hours. So that note means that given this event, even though the CRP was negative and the bloods didn't suggest the episode was highly unusual, and at that point in time I didn't know what was going on, so I wanted to put everything as a precaution in place.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, in babies, we don't always see an immediate CRP rise or a blood count rise. We do go on clinical signs, how the baby

blocks.text: Yes, I can. With newborn babies the umbilical vein, which is the vein that supplies blood before the baby is born, is a very easy access point for giving intravenous drugs or fluids.

blocks.text: So therefore it's much easier to put a cannula into an umbilical vein than to try and find a vein in an arm or leg. Therefore it's practical to pass a cannula into the umbilical vein.

blocks.text: Now, once it goes through the umbilical vein, you hope that it will go through into the vena cava.

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: And Dr Jayaram, I think, described it as being a perforation in the heart. Well, you tell us what a tamponade is.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The heart is surrounded by the pericardium. The pericardium is simply a lining around the heart. And usually there is no gap between the lining of the heart and the outside part of the heart tissue itself.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But if you can get -- if fluid or anything gets in between the outside of the heart and the inside of the pericardium, this lining, it will constrict and restrict the ability of the heart to contract properly, and it's literally a deadly serious condition. If there's enough fluid there, usually fluid -- could be blood, could be fluid -- then it restricts the heart contraction and, you know, will lead to a deterioration in the child's condition and death.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is there a clinically recognised potential connection between the insertion of a long line and a tamponade?

I'm sad to say
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: in Swansea we had a case of that nature where a baby died from cardiac tamponade.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So this is years and years ago and I'm not aware of any cases recently because of more care -- because of the awareness of this creeping phenomenon, but usually this is something that occurs in a long line that's been in for quite some time. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Heart rate, I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All doctors are familiar with dealing with patients of all ages who come in in a "collapsed" state to A&E where they've lost blood, you know, trauma. And in those cases -- or severe gastroenteritis in children, still common.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And in those babies, if they are severely ill as a result of loss of fluid, loss of, you know, diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of blood, the heart rate goes up.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So the heart rate was not high. The heart rate was pretty steady in [Baby A]'s case right until the time he collapsed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore although the failure to give him 4ml of fluid per hour --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think it's 4ml per kilo --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, for him it was per hour. Day 1 at 60ml per kilo per 24 hours. He was 1.6 kilo, so that's about 100ml per day. So 24 hours, it's 4ml per kilo. So that's the way we work it out.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore although he was devoid of fluid for 4 hours, the fact that he was on constant monitoring and the monitoring was great, you know, within normal limits, that was not an issue in relation to his collapsing.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay. Now, air embolus. How does an air embolus kill somebody? What is the mechanics of it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The mechanics is pretty straightforward. It interferes with the blood supply to the heart and lungs, to the lungs, and so the mechanism is the same as a clot from a -- that goes into the lung, what we know as a pulmonary embolus. It blocks off blood supply and kills you.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, we heard evidence concerning this purple or pink appearance that was -- that was flitting.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I want to ask you about an academic paper to which Dr Jayaram was referred yesterday. All right? I just would like to put that page up on the screen, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's the second page that he was shown. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we expand that left-hand column, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, you will remember, I'm sure, Dr Evans, that it was being suggested to Dr Jayaram yesterday that he in effect had lifted the explanation that appears in this academic paper and imposed it into his description. In other words, where it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "In one of our own cases we noted bright pink vessels against a generally cyanosed cutaneous background."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That was the part that was quoted to him yesterday.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I want to ask you about the next sentence, please. It reads on follows:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "This we attributed to direct oxygenation of erythrocytes..."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What is that word?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Erythrocytes, red blood cells.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "... adjacent to free air in the vascular system, while the tissues continued to be poorly perfused and oxygenated."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you translate that into language that I can understand, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It's straightforward, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Well, for you!
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Yes. First of all, just briefly about this paper, that is paper by Lee and Tanswell. And it's probably the best known paper in relation to pulmonary vascular air embolism in the newborn. It's published in 1989. So despite being over 30 years ago, it's a very well-known paper -- and the other reason it's well-known for British paediatricians is it was published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood, which is a monthly academic journal that all paediatricians receive.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore it's the most -- so the Archives are the most widely read journal from paediatricians.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Anyway, just to -- so this is not some obscure journal, you know, that nobody ever reads.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. In terms of this description, if babies collapse they become hypoxic, and the usual change in colour is they go blue. Okay? So they become cyanosed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If their blood pressure drops, they may go white.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You know, because there's no circulation. So therefore the colour changes you find in collapsed babies, collapsed children, is a combination of blue and white because they are white if there's no blood getting into the peripheries, into the skin, and they're blue if the blood that does get there is hypoxic, in other words lacking in oxygen. So that's what we're used to seeing in babies who collapse because of infection or any other cause, whatever.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore what we've got here is:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Bright pink vessels against a generally cyanosed cutaneous..."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You know, relating to the skin. So the fact that it's bright pink, now, that is remarkable. It's very unusual. It shouldn't be pink. You know, or if it's pink, why has the baby collapsed? It doesn't make sense.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Their interpretation is absolutely correct. They attribute it to the direct oxygenation of red blood cells -- in other words, red blood cells have got oxygen in them -- and adjacent to free air in the vascular system. In other words, there's air in the circulation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You know, air or oxygen in the circulation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So air is 21% oxygen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And air is 21% oxygen. So this is remarkable. You should never, ever, ever have air in your circulation because of -because it's dangerous.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And if the tissues continue to be purely perfused and oxygenated -- so they are really saying this makes no sense because we've got pink colouration and yet we've got collapsed patients. This shouldn't happen.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And they attribute it, quite correctly, to the fact that the cause is air embolism: air has got into the circulation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So it is the blood, essentially, unoxygenated, but the red blood cells oxygenate themselves from the air, in other words the 21% of the air, that's in the bloodstream?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's the answer?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, initially, Dr Evans, you offered a potential alternative cause of [Baby A]'s collapse and death. Can we just deal with that. First of all, what it was, and secondly, whether you still suggest that that is a possibility.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. Right. This was the -- the twins in the first cases I dealt with were presented in this way, and it's not a criticism. None of us knew what had happened. In other words, we were -you know, we just had no idea why these babies had collapsed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So one of -- so what crossed my mind was obstruction in breathing, smothering. The other possibility which I mentioned,
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: part of the differential diagnosis that we -- you know, that doctors do is that he'd received an injection of some noxious substance. But I just mentioned that, I have dismissed that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You're not suggesting that, on the evidence as you now know it to be, that that's a creditable alternative?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. If somebody asked me, give me five or six reasons why this baby could have collapsed, it would be one of the reasons. But no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, you finish your answer.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I finished.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can I just deal with a term that you have used because it's likely we're going to hear it again during the evidence, so I'm asking you to define a differential diagnosis.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What is a differential diagnosis to a medic?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. If you have a patient, any patient, who presents with an illness, there may well be three or four reasons to explain this illness. Babies are physiologically fairly simple individuals. So in a baby who has collapsed, the differential diagnosis would include hypoxia, lack of oxygen, sepsis, infection, airway obstruction, again causing hypoxia. So we would go through a list. We've discussed tamponade. That's another.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore there's a whole list of potential conditions that could compromise the stability of your baby. And that list of conditions is what we call a differential diagnosis.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. So is it another way in effect of putting what Dr Jayaram was articulating in the witness box yesterday, he was going through possibilities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is the method by which your profession, in effect, works in real time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It's thinking out loud.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Finally on [Baby A], please, Dr Evans, the means by which air could have been inserted into a baby's circulation. From what
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: you know of the way in which [Baby A] was being treated, what are the possibilities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, there are only two, really -- sorry, there's only one, really. The air would have gone through an intravenous line. And that can only occur in two ways: accidentally or on purpose. And that's it. Yes, so those are the only two explanations.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Some time ago I obtained a copy of all the intravenous bits and pieces of equipment used at the Chester hospital, which we're all familiar with. We are all familiar with these lines from visiting people in hospital, an intravenous bag line. I won't go through the whole bit.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But doctors, nurses, we're so obsessive about ensuring that air does not get into the system, you know, we're absolutely obsessive about it, and always have been, and it's much better now than -- So having rigged up the system that was used in Chester, and it's in a room in this court, in this building, so we could demonstrate it if necessary.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I rigged it all up. There's no way air could have got into [Baby A] by accident. You know, the fail-safe systems, the monitoring, the alarm set-ups, which have been present for, you know, a couple of decades, I suppose, ensures that this is not something that can occur accidentally.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Well, I'm going to recall you a bit later to deal with [Baby B]'s case if I may, and Mr Myers is putting over his questioning until we've dealt with [Baby B]. So those are all the questions I have at this stage.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So now Dr Bohin is coming in?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm just going to see -- do you want to have a short break before we carry on or do you want to carry on for another 40 minutes?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Right, good, we'll carry on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you for now, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So thank you, Dr Evans. That's it for the time being, but you will be coming back later, some time this afternoon. Thank you very much indeed. But take your documents with you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
DR SANDIE BOHIN (sworn)
Please do sit down. But you know the rules: voice up so that everyone can hear. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Would you identify yourself, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: My name is Dr Sandie Bohin.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you give the jury your list of qualifications, please, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I'm a member of the Royal College of Physicians and a fellow of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you qualify from Bristol University in the mid- 1980s?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And your professional career, please, took you to where and in what capacity?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I initially trained as a neonatologist, so that's a doctor who looks after small babies, but my general training as a junior doctor was in general paediatrics.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I chose to specialise in neonatology and when I was a senior registrar, I worked at the University of Leicester University Hospitals and was a locum consultant neonatologist there for a year before I got my substantive neonatal post.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then I worked from 1996, when I became a consultant, until the end of 2008 as a consultant neonatologist at the University Hospitals of Leicester.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's a large tertiary neonatal unit that covers 10,000 deliveries of babies and had about 600 admissions a year at that time. It covered all aspects of neonatology, including neonatal surgery and also covered a nearby cardiac unit which there was also in Leicester.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I became the head of service for that department shortly after becoming a consultant because, at that time, neonatal units didn't have large numbers of consultants like they have now. Now
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: most tertiary neonatal units would have probably a dozen consultants.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At that stage there were only three of us, and I think my colleagues were fed up of being the head of service, so I very quickly was given that job, and continued as head of service until I left in -- at the end of 2008.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And in 2009 I moved to Guernsey in the Channel Islands, so my career took a change. I became a consultant paediatrician with neonates, although the service there is very small and it's very different from the service that I was used to in the United Kingdom.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Guernsey is a Crown dependency and its health system is not the NHS, so it has a different health care system.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It has no junior doctors, and that is what attracted me to that role, because I wanted to get back to doing more hands-on stuff, which you don't actually do so much when you're a consultant in a very large teaching hospital, because you have junior doctors who do that role.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So since January 2009 I have worked as one of five consultants in Guernsey.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you retain any function within the NHS in England and Wales?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I do. Because the Guernsey healthcare system is very small, the population of Guernsey is very small, I was very conscious of the fact hay (sic) needed to keep skills up. In fact all the consultants in Guernsey do the same that I do and that is to spend time in the United Kingdom working in a specialist centre to keep their skills up, and I chose to -initially I did that for a year or so at the University of Southampton, because that's our nearest tertiary centre, but latterly, with the University of Bristol Regional Intensive Care Unit. And I go there anything from two to four weeks a year and I have an honorary contract with the University Hospitals of Bristol in order to do that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And when I go there I just do neonatal intensive care and high dependency and some transfers. That's important for me because I live on a small island and sick babies and children need to be transported to the mainland for specialist care, and I have an interest in transport and so I undertake transfers when I go to Bristol.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There was a hiatus, obviously, during COVID when I was not able travel because the island was locked down, but I have since resumed that area.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. And have you written and contributed to research papers and books and the like in this particular specialist field?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I certainly did in my -- when I was a junior doctor at the time I trained, because that was quite a long time ago, it was expected that you would carry out 2 years of research, which I did with Professor David Field, and some papers came as a result of that. And latterly I was asked to contribute to chapters in books on neonatal respiratory function, also on neonatal transport because I had set up the Neonatal Transport and Retrieval System in Leicester.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: My post was an NHS post, not an academic post, so I was not expected to write academic papers, but I certainly -- I did, but nothing since I have been in Guernsey.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Would you explain, please, to the jury the basis upon which you were retained in the context of this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I was approached by the National Crime Agency because I have done some work for them before, to peer-review some neonatal cases that have been undertaken by Dr Dewi Evans.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At that time the National Crime Agency had in fact engaged another neonatologist to do that work and he had peer-reviewed a few of the cases, but unfortunately he became seriously ill and was unable to continue with that work.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I was asked to peer-review cases that Dr Dewi who you have just heard from had written about, and I was asked to look at babies, the case notes and the cases of babies where there were concerns about collapses and deaths that people considered to be unusual, and I was asked to try and find a cause for potentially why they had collapsed and also to comment on whether I agreed with Dr Evans' findings, whether I disagreed with Dr Evans' findings, or if I, in fact, had found some additional findings myself.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as your reports are concerned, do they effectively follow that formula?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I didn't see any need to reproduce in detail the clinical history because that had already been done in Dr Dewi's
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: report. So my reports were, I guess, truncated and limited to what I felt were important parts of the history.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Like Dr Evans, were you provided with a series of documents which included the medical records relating to the child under consideration?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And those records of course included imaging; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And did you also, from time to time, not only see what Dr Evans had produced, but also what other experts had produced, not at least Dr Arthurs who the jury heard from last week?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: From a pathologist called Dr Andreas Marnerides, from whom the jury will hear in due course?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And indeed a statement from, in this particular, case from Professor Kinsey, who is a haematologist based in Leeds?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you also, so far as [Baby A]'s case was concerned, receive part of a witness statement that had been made by Dr Jayaram that was dated 18 September 2017?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. In your witness statement did you set out the chronology of [Baby A]'s life essentially from birth to death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that is in effect the chronology that has already been established by the evidence?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you in particular review the medical notes made by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And did you also, as I have said, see Dr Jayaram's notes?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And were you also given a post-mortem report written by Dr Shukla, who is based at Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as your opinion is concerned, what -- I'm now at section 5 of the report, my Lord, which is R, page 798?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: What conclusion did you draw relating to [Baby A]'s general well-being immediately prior to his collapse at about 20.20 hours on 8 June.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby A] was a baby who was 10 weeks early, but I think it's important to -- for the jury to understand that not all premature babies are the same, and that the more premature you are, the more problems you're likely to have.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby A] was 10 weeks early and so we would anticipate that he could possibly have some problems, but in fact he didn't really have any of those problems.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Immediately prior to his collapse he was what I would consider to be a stable baby. He was needing some respiratory support in the form of CPAP because he was a baby who was born early, but he wasn't in any oxygen, he was breathing in room air. He wasn't being troubled by apnoea of prematurity and wasn't unstable in that way. In fact, he was so well that the treating team decided that they would start to give him some feeds, and if he had been unstable in any way, that wouldn't have happened.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So looking at the observation charts that we've seen, his heart rate was stable throughout, his temperature was stable throughout, his respiratory rate in terms of breaths per minute was slightly at the upper end of normal, but was stable at that rate. So this wasn't an escalating respiratory rate. That was stable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He was handling well, and by that I mean that when the nurses routinely cared for him, changed his nappy, cleaned him, he didn't suddenly deteriorate.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So he tolerated all those -- all those things really very well. So he was extremely stable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. By "give him some feeds", are you referring to milk in this context?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He -- all premature babies have a very immature gut and it's very important that you don't suddenly feed them large amounts of milk as you would in a term baby.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So babies are given artificial nutrition in the form of parenteral nutrition, which we've previously heard about, and we know that that's important to give babies nutrition early on because they have a better outcome later on.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you can't do is give premature babies a total volume of feed in terms of their total fluids artificially, either by bottle, because premature babies have a poor suck reflex, or via the nasogastric tube, so the tube we have heard about that goes through the nose and down into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So what tends to happen is the majority of the nutrition is given intravenously by a long line or a UVC, while very slowly milk nutrition is given via the nasogastric tube. [Baby A] had been started on 1ml of breast milk every 2 hours via the nasogastric tube, and that's a tiny amount of milk, but it gets the tummy used to having nutrition in it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we deal with the issue of the umbilical venous catheter. Do you agree in effect with what Dr Evans said about that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I do. We have an umbilical catheter that we can show the jury if necessary. It's a very thin tube that, in the warmth of the neonatal unit, becomes very pliable. It's a very fine plastic tube, but neonatal units are very warm, babies are in incubators, which are also very warm, and it becomes very pliable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So you prime it. You fill it full of saline before you introduce it. Once you start to introduce it, you have no control over where it goes. You hope it stays in the main vein of the body, but it can veer off, and that's no criticism to the person putting in the tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's bad luck, really.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did that contribute to [Baby A]'s collapse or to his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The long line. We've heard from Dr Harkness about the position of that long line. In your opinion did the position of the long line make any contribution to [Baby A]'s collapse or to his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Now, we know that following the dextrose infusion being commenced at about 20.05 on the evening of 8 June, [Baby A] started to exhibit signs and ultimately stopped breathing, had an apnoea.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In your opinion did his stopping breathing have -- was that caused by his prematurity or some other cause?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Babies of 30 weeks' gestation can have apnoeas. An apnoea is defined as a pause of breathing of 20 seconds or more.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As Dr Evans said, their breathing is variable. So some babies at 30 weeks would possibly have a lot of problems with apnoea of prematurity, and the nurses would have noted that and would have recorded that in their observation charts.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby A] was not one of those babies that had had lots of problems with apnoea of prematurity. In fact, to counteract that, he'd been given caffeine, which is respiratory stimulant, which is routine practice. You can still have apnoeas despite having caffeine, but [Baby A] was not a baby that had had apnoeas before that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I think we can discount apnoea of prematurity in [Baby A], and then we are looking for apnoea for other causes, and they are the causes that Dr Evans has already gone through: hypoxia, infection, obstruction of the airway. But in my opinion I don't think any of those were pertinent to [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We have heard and you have heard of details of the striking discolouration of [Baby A]'s skin, in particular I think the source of that information so far as you were concerned was Dr Jayaram's statement. What in your opinion caused that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are potentially lots of causes for rashes in babies, particularly babies who have collapsed in the way that [Baby A] did, and unfortunately if you see lots of babies who have collapsed, you are aware that they are grey-y blue. They may be white. But they don't have the type of rash that was described in [Baby A] with this pink blotchy rash that seemed to fluctuate and come and go. So in my experience things like infection, sepsis and hypoxia would not cause that type of rash.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So what are the possibilities for causing that type of rash and a subsequent death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, I came to the conclusion, looking at a differential diagnosis, excluding the other things, I was left with air embolus as being the cause of this sort of rash with this pink/purple blotchiness that seemed to come on very, very quickly at the time that [Baby A] collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I was left with the only -- the plausible explanation being that of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Now, knowing what you know about the way in which long lines are managed in the NHS, did you consider whether or not the air embolus could have been the result of an accident?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, air can only get in one of two ways: either accidentally or deliberately. My experience is that nursing staff and medical staff who either put in the lines or who subsequently care for the lines and change fluids are absolutely meticulous to prevent any air getting into those lines.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the lines and the little connecting ports are all filled with saline so that there is no -- even the tiniest air bubble can't get into the line. It's something that is just ingrained in nursing and medical staff.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I think the accidental administration or air getting in accidentally, I think, is -- is extremely unlikely, extremely unlikely.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In addition, the pumps that are used to administer bags of fluid have an alarm on them. So from the bag to the pump -- the tubing goes from the bag to the pump and then on to the patient. Those pumps have alarms that will detect air coming down the line. blocks.text: Yes. Have there been studies dealing with volume and speed of emboluses?
